# Results — Study 495 (Kagi Charts)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **the Kagi
line turning yang (thick) marks a confirmed uptrend, so buy the yang switch** — encoded as a
mechanical rule. The Kagi line is built bar-by-bar from closes (no future data); it reverses on
a 4% counter-move and switches thickness at the prior shoulder/waist; a long fires on the bar
the line turns **yang** (thin→thick, an up-break of the prior shoulder), entered at the **next
close** (one documented lag), and we measure the forward 5/10/20/60-day return. Offline &
deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| Entries | **144** mechanical yang switches pooled across the 5 tapes (reversal = 4%) |
| Timing / costs | Kagi line uses closes up to *t*; yang switch read on close of *t*; enter the **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per switch |

> **Price-only vs total-return.** The ETFs are auto-adjusted (dividends reinvested) — labelled
> total-return everywhere. The Signal axis uses a basket of **surviving** liquid ETFs; this is a
> single-instrument trend study, not a cross-sectional anomaly, so survivorship affects only the
> drift baseline (which is exactly what the random-entry control neutralizes).

## The signal — yang switch vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number (it measures the index's upward drift); the
**Welch switch-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters. Δ = switch − random.

| horizon | n | switch | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (switch−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 144 | +22.2 bps | 58% | +1.10 | +10.3 bps | **+11.9 bps** | +20.2 bps | +0.41 | 0.682 |
| 10-day | 143 | +22.8 bps | 58% | +0.65 | +53.6 bps | **−30.8 bps** | +20.8 bps | −0.71 | 0.477 |
| 20-day | 143 | +88.7 bps | 57% | +1.81 | +33.1 bps | **+55.6 bps** | +86.7 bps | +0.92 | 0.358 |
| 60-day | 140 | +253.3 bps | 60% | +2.84 | +118.9 bps | **+134.3 bps** | +251.3 bps | +1.27 | 0.205 |

Read it carefully. The one-sample *t* against zero nudges up with the horizon (**+2.84** at 60
days) — but that is **drift**: long-only entries on an upward-drifting index inherit the tide.
Against the **drift-matched random baseline**, the yang switch is *worse* at 10 days
(Δ = −30.8 bps) and only nominally better elsewhere (+11.9 / +55.6 / +134.3 bps). The
switch-minus-random difference **never clears the desk's *t* ≥ 2 bar** (max Welch *t* = +1.27 at
60 days, *p* = 0.205). The yang switch does not forecast.

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — a positive sign but no significance anywhere

| ticker | entries | switch | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (switch−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 24 | +117.2 bps | +0.99 | +39.3 bps | **+77.9 bps** |
| QQQ | 29 | +75.2 bps | +0.54 | +88.2 bps | **−13.0 bps** |
| IWM | 39 | +85.0 bps | +0.69 | +2.7 bps | **+82.4 bps** |
| DIA | 26 | +146.7 bps | +1.69 | +33.7 bps | **+112.9 bps** |
| GLD | 26 | +26.9 bps | +0.40 | +1.5 bps | **+25.4 bps** |

The delta is positive in 4 of 5 names — but every single per-ticker one-sample *t* is **below
1.7**, and the pooled Welch test (above) never reaches 2. With only ~24–39 switches per
instrument over 21 years, this is exactly the noisy, underpowered signature you'd expect when a
rule re-describes the same long-run drift. No instrument carries a stand-alone edge.

## Geometry placebo — re-parameterise the Kagi, nothing changes

The decisive "does the geometry matter?" test: rebuild the Kagi line with a **randomly drawn
reversal threshold** (1%–8%, the span of common Kagi defaults), keeping the same price marginal
and a comparable switch frequency. If price genuinely respected *this specific* 4% Kagi's
shoulders and waists, a randomly-parameterised Kagi should do much worse.

| test | observed yang-switch 20d return | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY threshold-scramble Kagi | +117.2 bps | **0.545** | 500 |

**55% of randomly-parameterised Kagis match or beat the real 4% one** (*p* = 0.545). The
specific shoulder/waist geometry carries no information — any plausible Kagi does as well.
"The yang switch confirms a trend" is busted.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real momentum burst

On a deterministic tape with a *planted* post-yang-switch momentum burst (knob `edge`), the
same yang-switch rule behaves exactly as it must — so the flat real-tape result is a genuine
"nothing there", not a dead detector.

| planted edge | n | switch | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no burst) | 38 | +82.7 bps | 53% | +1.25 |
| **0.25** (real planted burst) | 30 | +464.8 bps | 80% | **+7.47** |

With no planted burst the control sits below *t* = 2 (no false positive); a real planted
momentum burst lights up at *t* = +7.47 with an 80% win-rate. The detector is live.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The yang switch does **not** beat a drift-matched random baseline
  (switch − random = +11.9 / −30.8 / +55.6 / +134.3 bps at 5/10/20/60 days; the switch-vs-random
  Welch *t* never clears 2, max +1.27 at 60 days, *p* = 0.205). The mild one-sample *t* at 60
  days (+2.84) is drift — the upward climb of long equity indices, inherited by any long-only
  rule.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is no residual edge once the drift you were always getting is
  removed, and costs only deepen the hole. The same drift is captured more cheaply and more
  fully by holding the index; the Kagi rule trades less, sits out of the market on yin, and pays
  costs on each switch, dominating nothing. No capacity question because there is no edge to
  scale.
- **"Do Kagi reversals time the market"? — BUSTED.** The threshold-scramble placebo leaves the
  result intact (*p* = 0.545): randomly-parameterised Kagis do as well as the real 4% one, so the
  specific shoulders and waists carry no forecasting information. The Kagi chart is a descriptive
  noise-filter, not a market-timing strategy.
